Question: What is something that you read recently and is worth sharing?
Answer: I’ve been reading a book called The World That Never Was: A True Story of Dreamers, Schemers, Anarchists, and Secret Agents: Butterworth, Alex: 9780307386755: Amazon.com: Books There are some fascinating stories in this book, and I’m going to share one of my favorites…read to the end, it’s worth it…Trust Me! This is Louis Lingg, he was born in Germany in 1864. His family didn’t have alot of money. His dad worked at a lumber mill. One day his dad was moving logs on the river and it was icy. His dad fell through the ice and was trapped for a while, but was rescued. After the accident, his dad wasn’t able to perform all the tasks at his job as well as he could before…the lumber mill fired him after working there for over 20 years. (His dad passed away 3 years later) Seeing how his father was treated set him on his path of radicalization and anarchy. He immigrated to the United States in 1885 and settled in Chicago. He developed a reputation as a supporter of anarchism. He was elected to the Central Labor Union and devoted his time to the cause. On May 4, 1886 around 3000 people showed up in protest and solidarity of an 8 hour workday, and the shooting of some workers by police previously. Police tried to get the crowd to disperse, when someone threw a bomb into the crowd. It killed 8 men and wounded over 60 people. Louis Lingg was one of 8 men eventually arrested for the bombing. There were several witnesses that stated that Lingg was not the person that threw the bomb. And in Lingg’s testimony, he stated he could not have beent he one to throw the bomb because he was at home, making bombs for a different occassion! They were all sentenced to death. Well…Louis decided he did not want to die by hanging. Somehow some bombs were smuggled into the prison, but the guards ended up finding and confiscating them. Louis had removed the blasting caps from them and put them in his mouth like a cigar, and lit them. It blew off his jaw and half of his face, and he ended up dying around 3pm later that day. On June 26, 1893 the governor of Illinois pardoned all 8 men saying they are innocent. They were all buried beneath the Haymarket Martys Monument in Forest Park, IL. On a fun side note…there is a punk rock band formed in 2006 from Paris, France called Louis Lingg and The Bombs. Louis Lingg and the Bombs

Question: What did your grandparents used to do?
Answer: So not exactly my grandparents, but my husbands. They both were amazing people. He was a newspaper editor and she was a tole painter in West Virginia. They traveled the world and did exactly what they wanted This is going to be long…I rarely get a chance to talk about them :) But I promise, it’s worth it! He started as a “cub reporter” for the newspaper in Charleston, WV and worked his way up. He worked at the Charleston Daily Mail. He wrote a lot of commentary…like the article below. This is one of my favorites. He wrote an almost weekly newspaper article in 1975 and 1976 called “Nature’s Window” and would talk about things they had seen on their adventures. She would illustrate it with the subject of his article. The family has all the original prints of her artwork for all the articles. They are beautiful, colorful pieces of art that are all frame-worthy by themselves. Mary also was invited to paint Easter Eggs representing her state of West Virginia for the White House Easter Egg Roll during Reagan’s presidency in 1987. No, they did not get “rolled” :) Today, her eggs are located in the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library in Simi Valley, CA. One day, we hope to be able to go and see them. The Registrar of the library told me that if we decide to come out around Easter, they can make sure they are on display. We also have so many beautiful pieces she painted throughout her life. The family were all gifted with pieces during their life, and were split up among family after her death. Here are some of the pieces that we have. I just love looking at them and love the tole style of painting and the detail in her work. I really hope you’ve enjoyed reading this. Question: How do you define a "soccer mom," and is there a "soccer dad"?
Answer: I’ve almost answered this question about a dozen times. My answer almost always is snarky and criticizing of most of the other answers, and I try not to do that, so I’ve always just erased it. The way most describe “soccer mom” is unflattering. I wonder if they know any personally, or are just answering based on basic stereotypes? Instead, I’m going to tell you about my experience as a soccer mom. My son has played soccer for almost 6 years. To me, a soccer mom is just a mom who has a kid that plays soccer. 98% of the moms I’ve met through my sons soccer are not what I see most people describing. Almost all of them (that I know) have full time jobs outside of the home. Customer Service, Stylist, Teacher, Account Managers, Accountants, Firefighter, Paralegal, Insurance Agent, Social Worker. They are not married to ultra-rich men and drive huge SUV’s. They do not scream and yell at their kids during games and/or practices. (I know one lady who does this for an opposing team and always make sure I am no where around her) They don’t push their kids to play soccer, don’t schedule every second of their kids time in soccer, and don’t live their live revolving around it. Honestly, now that I’ve started writing, it irritates me the more I think about it. I love my fellow “soccer moms” who want what their kid wants. Works through lunch so they can leave early to get their kid to practice on time. Sits in the car during practices on their laptops to make up work from leaving early. Volunteers to record games for other parents who can’t attend, car pools kids to and from games/practices for parents who can’t make it. Make sure all the kids have snacks, water, sunscreen (these are 9/10 year olds) gloves, jackets. Provide canopies and benches for the team and lugs them to each game. Sounds like a bunch of horrible people to me 🙄🙄

Question: Do mentally disabled people live long?
Answer: This is hard to answer because there’s such a wide range of “mentally disabled” with multitudes of diagnoses. I’m going to speak for people who have the chromosome disorder that my daughter has, Jacobsen Syndrome. [1] Jacobsen's Syndrome (11q Deletion or 11q-) is a rare chrome disorder in which a portion of the 11th chromosome is missing. It affects about one in every 100,000 births. People who have this disorder may have heart problems, speech and language problems, specific facial characteristics, and mild to severe mental retardation, although many children with Jacobsen's are extremely capable. Jacobsen Syndrome is caused by the loss of a small portion of a chromosome at conception. A chromosome is made up of DNA code in a thread-like structure present in the nucleus of most cells in the body. The DNA code in turn carry genes which are the all important instructions about how each cell in the body should divide, grow and die. In each cell, there are 23 pairs of chromosomes. The body needs all 23 pairs for normal health and development. In Jacobsen Syndrome a small piece of the 11th chromosome is missing (or deleted) and this causes a range of clinical features in individuals with this condition. The features are related to the genes that are absent from the small piece of chromosome 11 that is missing. The reason for the loss of the piece of chromosome is not fully understood. Jacobsen syndrome tends to occur more frequently in females than in males. [2] In the case of Jacobsen Syndrome, your medical issues are directly related to the amount of the 11th chromosome is missing and where it is. A lot of the kids that have this have heart defects. One of those defects is HLHS (Hypoplastic Left Heart), which is a congenital heart defect where the left side of the heart doesn’t form correctly. There are several babies/toddlers that have passed away from this. I also know of people well into middle-age adulthood who have this. There is one mom who had a child with Jacobsen Syndrome, so the parents had genetic testing done, and turns out the Mom had Jacobsen Syndrome as well, and had no idea. This mom was in her twenties, had graduated from college and had a great job. Each case is so unique and special. And this includes not just this particular diagnosis, but is true for most diagnosis.

Question: What is the most frightening moment you have ever experienced?
Answer: That would be the birth of my daughter, and the subsequent couple of weeks afterward Mainly, finding out she had a rare chromosome disorder. My daughter, Kaylee, was born in September 1998 by cesarean section. Up to the moment of her birth, we had no idea that anything was wrong with her. Ultrasounds were normal, and we were thrilled. My own little bundle of joy to cuddle and love. I was ecstatic! Her due date was September 23rd. September 23rd came and went, and still no baby. I went to what I hoped was my last OB appointment on September 30th. We found out that she had turned around and was now in a breach position. She was a small baby, so the doctor said she had plenty of room to move around and was basically turning somersaults in my stomach. She went ahead and sent me to the hospital to finally bring her into the world. They predicted that she would turn around once I was on Pitocin and everything was going to be fine. The drive to the hospital was filled with joyous phone calls and nervous chatter. I couldn't believe the big moment was finally here. I got checked in, put into a room, IV started, and they started the Pitocin. Everything was going smoothly, until the doctor came in for the exam. The good news was that she had turned around head first The bad news was that the umbilical chord was around her neck so it was decided that a cesarean section was the logical answer. At this point, I was nervous and scared for my baby. Laying on the table in the OR and waiting for them to get her out felt like an eternity. I could tell the moment they pulled her out and saw her that something just wasn't right. The air seemed to go out of the room, and I thought I was going to pass out. But they wrapped her up and brought her over for me to see her. To me, she was the most beautiful baby I had ever seen, She was so tiny. Only 6 lb, 1 oz., and 18" long. I was sent to recovery for what seemed like forever, but was really less than 2 hours. I was moved into a room and waiting anxiously for her. When they finally wheeled her in she was in an incubator, and I wasn't allowed to hold her. Only reach through a hole in the side and touch her. She had petechiae all over her body. They were small purple bruising spots the size of pencil lead. I remember just wanting to be able to hold her, but she was being transported to the University of Kentucky Children's Hospital. That's when the hardest part started. I was stuck in a hospital 30 miles away from where my baby was being taken. I had just had surgery and wasn't allowed to leave the hospital until I had recovered. She needed me, and I needed her. It broke my heart when they wheeled her out and I knew I wouldn't be able to see her for 2 days until I was released from the hospital. Those were the longest 2 days of my life. 1 couldn't wait to get to see my angel again. Finally the time came and we went straight to the Children's Hospital. There was my little precious girl, in an incubator, under a jaundice lamp, with coverings over her eyes and an IV in her head. I couldn't stop the tears from flowing down my face. I was told that they weren't sure what was wrong with her, but had taken blood and had started running test after test. Her heels were bandaged up where they had to take a razor blade and slice them to get blood for the tests. The IV was in her head because they couldn't get it in here small veins in her arms. I vividly remember the first time I got to hold her...getting all the tubes and wires out of the way so I could situate her in my lap to feed her. I would just sit and hold her and stare at her, and fall more in love with her by the minute. Days later, she was finally done with the jaundice lamps and was placed in a regular bed. I would have spent the night there if they would have let me, I would get up in the morning, stay all day, and come home late at night. I hated when I had to leave her at night. We had multiple conversations with neurologists, cardiologists, and geneticists. I had 10 tubes of blood taken to run a barrage of tests to see if it was genetic. Finally after 6 days in the hospital, it had a name. Jacobsen Syndrome or 11q terminal deletion[1] . I had never heard of Jacobsen Syndrome, and neither had almost anybody else at the hospital. We were lucky to get her diagnosis so early. Some people find out years later what their children have. It was a relief just to have a name to put with it. After 10 days in the hospital, they released Kaylee to come home with us. She was eating well, gaining weight slowly, and there was nothing else they could do for her in the hospital. We left the hospital without really knowing what was going to happen. Would I be able to take care of her? Was I capable being a good mom to a child that was "different"? I soon realized that I didn't have anything to worry about. She was a fantastic baby! She ate well, slept well, and was adored by everyone in the house. We had regular doctor appointments to check on her progress. When she was around 7 months old, it was recommended that she start physical and occupational therapy. We started going 2 times a week, but I couldn't see that she was making progress. She cried the whole time and so we stopped going. For the most part, Kaylee is very healthy. She has Paris-Trousseau syndrome, which is a bleeding disorder. Approximately 90% of kids with Jacobsen Syndrome have this. It can cause abnormal bleeding and easy bruising. She bruises easily from bumping into things or falling down, but her blood clots well enough that it's not a major concern anymore. She has had strabismus surgery two times. Strabismus is a disorder where the eyes do not line up correctly, resulting in crossed or lazy eye. She had to have the muscles tightened in both of her eyes and although they are not perfect, it has helped tremendously. She has a heart murmur, and goes for an EKG and Echo cardiogram every couple of years to check everything out. Congenital heart disease is present in about half of all diagnosed Jacobsen Syndrome kids. We feel very blessed that so far she has not developed this complication, as it can develop later in life. Kaylee has occupational, physical and speech therapy at school. She officially graduated last year, but gets to continue going to this school until she is 21. To say that she loves school is an understatement. She is constantly signing "school" and is ready to go back as soon as she is picked up. She loves her teachers who have been fantastic in setting goals for her and helping her to achieve them. We've had a few rough spots a time or two, but overall her school experience has been wonderful. I feel so blessed to have Kaylee in my life. She has made me a better person without even knowing it or trying to, She is the sweetest, funniest, most loving child a parent could ask for. I never get tired of her giving me "squeezes" and wanting to ride on my back to go upstairs to brush her teeth and get ready for bed. She loves her blankie, chocolate milk. I look at her sometimes and tears well up in my eyes just thinking about how far she has came in her 19 years, and I wouldn't change a thing.

Question: What is a classroom for the medically fragile/multiply handicapped like?

They have a yoga room in the classroom and do yoga videos from YouTube. The kids love it! There are peer tutors that come into the classroom to help the kids. For the peer tutors, it is an elected class that they have to apply and interview for. About 95% of the peer tutors go on to become special ed teachers, therapists or social workers. There are several aides in the classroom that help out as well. They have a supermarket section where they practice money handling and counting. Just this last week they dissected owl pellets. They do a lot of hands on activities. They focus a lot on activities towards independence. Tying shoes, putting on coats independently, brushing hair and teeth. Question: Will my life be ruined if I have a disabled child?

How financially stable were you before the disabled child came along? There are so many things labeled “disabled” that the degree and severity is going to come into play. There are MANY people that are “disabled” that have the ability to be partially independent, either at home or at a care facility. They work, go to school, live semi-independently, participate in activities just like everyone else. Yes, being the caretaker for someone that is considered disabled is a lot of work. Yes, you will make sacrifices for that child. Yes, there will be days that all you want to do is cry and stay in bed. Yes, many days you will feel like you are at the end of your rope. But guess what? There will also be good days. Days that your child meets a goal they’ve been working towards for months. Days when they’ve learned a new word or sign and are proud of themselves, and want you to be proud of them. Days when their face lights up when they see you, and run to you to give you a big hug. Days when they graduate from high school, and walk across the stage and get their diploma. With their family, friends, teachers and peers cheering. With smiles and happy tears. It’s HARD. But that doesn’t mean it’s not worth it.

The last time that led to my cancellation was that I recieved ingredients, but the recipe cards inside the box did not match the ingredients I recieved. It wasn’t the biggest deal, but I just decided that I would quit for a while. I cancelled the end of October and haven’t started it back up yet. Question: How do you help your children adjust to having a sibling with special needs and not develop resentment towards them and the extra care they may need?

Until he was around 3, he had no idea that his sister was any different. He went with me to her PT and OT appointments. To him, it was just “the place he got to play with all the train tracks” Around three is when he started asking me why his sister didn’t talk, why she didn’t play with toys, why she made weird noises (his words) We just simply told him that his sister was special, and will always need a little extra help. Because she sometimes requires “extra” attention and care, we balance it with him by taking him to do special activities alone. Most of these activities are things his sister would most definitely NOT enjoy anyway…so we take his sister to grandmas, and we spend time with him. We went to Monster Jam - he loves Gravedigger! We took him to LegoLand because he’s a Lego fanatic. He loves his sister, and he is so patient and helpful with her. He will hold her hand and help her up steps. He says “Come on sissy” when she’s lagging behind, and he’ll grab her hand to pull her along. We always tell him if he feels like he needs attention, to just tell us. We try our best, but sometimes he may feel left out. And he’s good about coming to me every now and then and saying “Mom, I need some attention”

Question: What's your story of being pregnant?
Answer: By now, we are used to the sideways glances and blatant stares by both children and adults. You would think my daughter had 2 heads and tentacles for arms by the way people stare at her. Sometimes I ignore it; sometimes I stare right back at them until they make eye Contact with me and quickly look away. I guess that's the way of the world. She has no idea that people are staring, nor does she care. She is beautiful, happy and the greatest gift that I have ever received. My daughter, Kaylee, was born in September 1998 by cesarean section. Up to the moment of her birth, we had no idea that anything was wrong with her. Ultrasounds were normal, and we were thrilled. My own little bundle of joy to coddle and love. I was ecstatic! Her due date was September 23rd. September 23rd came and went, and still no baby. I went to what I hoped was my last OB appointment on September 30th. We found out that she had turned around and was now in a breach position. She was a small baby, so the doctor said she had plenty of room to move around and was basically turning somersaults in my stomach. She went ahead and sent me to the hospital to finally bring her into the world. They predicted that she would turn around once I was on Pitocin and everything was going to be fine. The drive to the hospital was filled with joyous phone calls and nervous chatter. I couldn't believe the big moment was finally here. I got checked in, put into a room, IV started, and they started the Pitocin. Everything was going smoothly, until the doctor came in for the exam. The good news was that she had turned around head first The bad news was that the umbilical chord was around her neck so it was decided that a cesarean section was the logical answer. At this point, I was nervous and scared for my baby. Laying on the table in the OR and waiting for them to get her out felt like an eternity. I could tell the moment they pulled her out and saw her that something just wasn't right. The air seemed to go out of the room, and I thought I was going to pass out. But they wrapped her up and brought her over for me to see her. To me, she was the most beautiful baby I had ever seen, She was so tiny. Only 6 lb, 1 oz., and 18" long. I was sent to recovery for what seemed like forever, but was really less than 2 hours. I was moved into a room and waiting anxiously for her. When they finally wheeled her in she was in an incubator, and I wasn't allowed to hold her. Only reach through a hole in the side and touch her. She had petechiae all over her body. They were small purple bruising spots the size of pencil lead. I remember just wanting to be able to hold her, but she was being transported to the University of Kentucky Children's Hospital. That's when the hardest part started. I was stuck in a hospital 30 miles away from where my baby was being taken. I had just had surgery and wasn't allowed to leave the hospital until I had recovered. She needed me, and I needed her. It broke my heart when they wheeled her out and I knew I wouldn't be able to see her for 2 days until I was released from the hospital. Those were the longest 2 days of my life. 1 couldn't wait to get to see my angel again. Finally the time came and we went straight to the Children's Hospital. There was my little precious girl, in an incubator, under a jaundice lamp, with coverings over her eyes and an IV in her head. I couldn't stop the tears from flowing down my face. I was told that they weren't sure what was wrong with her, but had taken blood and had started running test after test. Her heels were bandaged up where they had to take a razor blade and slice them to get blood for the tests. The IV was in her head because they couldn't get it in here small veins in her arms. I vividly remember the first time I got to hold her...getting all the tubes and wires out of the way so I could situate her in my lap to feed her. I would just sit and hold her and stare at her, and fall more in love with her by the minute. Days later, she was finally done with the jaundice lamps and was placed in a regular bed. I would have spent the night there if they would have let me, I would get up in the morning, stay all day, and come home late at night. I hated when I had to leave her at night. We had multiple conversations with neurologists, cardiologists, and geneticists. I had 10 tubes of blood taken to run a barrage of tests to see if it was genetic. Finally after 6 days in the hospital, it had a name. Jacobsen Syndrome or 11q terminal deletion[1] . I had never heard of Jacobsen Syndrome, and neither had almost anybody else at the hospital. We were lucky to get her diagnosis so early. Some people find out years later what their children have. It was a relief just to have a name to put with it. After 10 days in the hospital, they released Kaylee to come home with us. She was eating well, gaining weight slowly, and there was nothing else they could do for her in the hospital. We left the hospital without really knowing what was going to happen. Would I be able to take care of her? Was I capable being a good mom to a child that was "different"? I soon realized that I didn't have anything to worry about. She was a fantastic baby! She ate well, slept well, and was adored by everyone in the house. We had regular doctor appointments to check on her progress. When she was around 7 months old, it was recommended that she start physical and occupational therapy. We started going 2 times a week, but I couldn't see that she was making progress. She cried the whole time and so we stopped going. For the most part, Kaylee is very healthy. She has Paris-Trousseau syndrome, which is a bleeding disorder. Approximately 90% of kids with Jacobsen Syndrome have this. It can cause abnormal bleeding and easy bruising. She bruises easily from bumping into things or falling down, but her blood clots well enough that it's not a major concern anymore. She has had strabismus surgery two times. Strabismus is a disorder where the ayes do not line up correctly, resulting in crossed or lazy eye. She had to have the muscles tightened in both of her eyes and although they are not perfect, it has helped tremendously. She has a heart murmur, and goes for an EKG and Echo cardiogram every couple of years to check everything out. Congenital heart disease is present in about half of all diagnosed Jacobsen Syndrome kids. We feel very blessed that so far she has not developed this complication, as it can develop later in life. Kaylee has occupational, physical and speech therapy at school. She officially graduated last year, but gets to continue going to this school until she is 21. To say that she loves school is an understatement. She is constantly signing "school" and is ready to go back as soon as she is picked up. She loves her teachers who have been fantastic in setting goals for her and helping her to achieve them. We've had a few rough spots a time or two, but overall her school experience has been wonderful. I feel so blessed to have Kaylee in my life. She has made me a better person without even knowing it or trying to, She is the sweetest, funniest, most loving child a parent could ask for. I never get tired of her giving me "squeezes" and wanting to ride on my back to go upstairs to brush her teeth and get ready for bed. She loves her blankie, chocolate milk, The Wonder Pets, and shredding Ziploc freezer bags (no seriously, she SHREDS them, look at the picture below). I look at her sometimes and tears well up in my eyes just thinking about how far she has came in her 19 years, and I wouldn't change a thing.

Question: How do you downsize your kids' toy collection when they have too many?
Answer: I have a couple of methods that have worked pretty well for us. We started doing this a couple of years ago, a couple of times a year. Usually in June (his birthday month) and in December. DONATE TO A CLASSROOM My daughter is special needs. She had a teacher in elementary school that we still keep in touch with and see occasionally. This year when we were going through his toys, we asked if he’d like to give the toys to Mrs. **** for her classroom. He enthusiastically went through his toys after that and we talked about if it would be a good toy for a classroom. We then texted pictures of everything to the teacher and she told us what she would like. She was very appreciative and she took almost everything we had. So check with teachers to see if they can use things you are getting rid of. Especially puzzles, games, blocks, costumes, kids furniture. YARD SALE Our neighborhood has 2 yard sales every year. We use this opportunity to downsize. My son goes through his things, and he gets to keep the money from the sale of his toys. He carefully selects toys that he wants to get rid of. He gets to buy one new toy with the money, and the rest goes in his bank. This is after the last purge. Still way too much stuff…but much less than before.

Question: What is the typical experience like for special needs children who attend inclusive public school classes?
Answer: I live in the state of Kentucky in the United States, so I can speak for our experience. My daughter attends public school and started when she was 4, with preschool. She has always received occupational, physical, and speech therapy at school. She has received help with assistive technology. She’s had an IEP since we started preschool and we revisit it annually and discuss goals and change anything we need to. We also have a yearly Annual Review and talk about progress. I just had her ARC last week and it was decided she no longer needs speech services as they have been. She officially “graduated” from high school in May 2017, but she gets to continue to go to this school until she is 21. She spends some of her time in a regular classroom, but the majority is spent in a modified classroom. She does activities that are modified for her and the other kids. There are peer tutors that come to every class to help her. They help her with work, they help her get to her next class, they help her get her lunch. She has a “job” that she goes to on Tuesdays and Thursdays. She is a greeter at WalMart. Since she is very social and LOVES people, this is the perfect job for her. She gets to say Hi to people for hours! Sometimes she also helps to put things back on racks or shelves. Every Friday they have a CBI trip. CBI is Community Based Instruction. They go to a store or a restaurant. They have their own money and purchase items or food. They learn about money management and on counting their money. In December they will go to the mall and get Christmas presents for their family. They do yoga during the week. My daughter has become the unofficial leader of yoga. She tells everyone it’s time to take their shoes off, and to get on the floor. She has the yoga routine memorized and even leads it. Our experience overall has been wonderful. There have been bumps in the road, and we’ve dealt with those. We are lucky that the special education program in our school district is fantastic!

Question: What do parents feel about their children with disabilities? Do they ever hate them or see them as a burden?
Answer: Yeah, I’m having a pity party as we speak. (Yes, sarcasm) I never hate my daughter, nor do I see her as a burden. I love her equally to my “normal” (i hate that word) child. How can I hate a child who is an innocent soul? She has no malice towards anyone. She isn’t spiteful, spoiled, bratty, deceitful, mean. Does she require more care and more of my time than my other child? YES But that doesn’t make her a burden. If anything, we’ve met more people and done many more things that we normally would not have done if we didn’t have her. Look at that face! :-)
